query: Which material can be used for to improve the ductility and toughness of the HfZrTi high-entropy alloy (HEAs), and why?

generation.hypothesis: Small, carefully controlled additions of interstitial oxygen (approximately 1–2 at%) to HfZrTi will improve its ductility and toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfZrTi high-entropy alloy with a single-phase microstructure
generation.intervention: Incorporation of ~1–2 at% oxygen during alloy synthesis or processing
generation.conditions: Melt alloying under controlled atmosphere to ensure uniform oxygen distribution, followed by standard solidification and thermomechanical treatments
generation.structural_mediator: Interstitial oxygen incorporation leading to short-range ordering and enhanced slip
generation.mechanism: Oxygen atoms occupying interstitial sites in HfZrTi reduce localized lattice distortions and improve slip transfer, resulting in increased plasticity and crack tolerance
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline undoped alloy, ductility should improve by roughly 10% or more, along with a slight increase in strength
generation.baseline: Undoped HfZrTi generally exhibits limited tensile elongation (<10%)
generation.boundary: Excess oxygen levels above ~2 at% may lead to embrittlement and degrade mechanical properties
generation.uncertainty: Precise optimal oxygen content and large-scale processing routes remain unvalidated and could affect final properties

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize HfZrTi samples with varying oxygen contents from 0 to 3 at% and measure tensile properties before and after solution treatment. Compare elongation, strength, and fracture behavior.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxygen-doped HfZrTi alloys fail to show improved ductility or toughness relative to the undoped baseline, the hypothesis is invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: We observed that the relaxation peaks in the current HEAs are asymmetrically broadened (see Fig. 1, A to C ). This is a feature associated with the variety of interstitial relaxation processes involved in these massive solid solutions ( [28] ). Because of the complexity in alloy composition and the resulting multitude in local chemical environments in which the interstitial atoms switch their positions, it is difficult to conduct a complete peak deconvolution analysis based on all possible individual relaxation processes. However, two main configurations of the interstitial atoms can indeed be distinguished in the current material, namely, position switches of interstitials in ordered interstitial complexes and relaxation of randomly distributed interstitial atoms ( [22] ). These two kinds of configurations both contribute to the current Snoek relaxation and can cause at least some of the asymmetries observed. Therefore, we conduct a decomposition of the relaxation structure in terms of the two main classes of interstitial configurations (see the Supplementary Materials). decision.trend: A study on a Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi-based high-entropy alloy (reference PMC7299626) demonstrated that small interstitial additions of oxygen or nitrogen can raise strength, but oxygen in particular also significantly increases plasticity—improving ductility from 10.8% to about 20% elongation. Although this approach overcame some inherent limitations in ductility and toughness, questions remain regarding the optimal level of interstitials and the effect of uniformity in larger-scale processing.
decision.unsolved: While low-level oxygen additions clearly enhance ductility and toughness, challenges remain in fine-tuning the exact oxygen content for optimal mechanical properties and ensuring emergent phases and microstructures remain stable under service conditions and manufacturing scales.
decision.lever: Controlled interstitial oxygen additions (approximately 1–2 at%) to HfZrTi to exploit short-range ordering and interstitial strengthening without embrittlement
decision.why: Prior work in a related Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi system shows that small, carefully controlled additions of oxygen simultaneously increase yield strength and improve ductility, indicating that the same approach is likely beneficial for enhancing toughness in HfZrTi-based HEAs.
